description: Positive, negative, intrinsic, extrinsic and knowledge of results or performance feedback.
content_html:
Why Feedback Matters in Sport

Every time a gymnast sticks a landing, a coach calls a correction, or a tennis player hears the crowd react to a shot, information is flowing. That information — feedback — is at the heart of how athletes learn, refine skills and progress. Without it, performers would repeat errors indefinitely. With the right type of feedback, delivered at the right moment, improvement accelerates.

The specification organises feedback into three overlapping categories: its emotional tone (positive or negative), its source (intrinsic or extrinsic), and what it tells you (knowledge of results or knowledge of performance). A single piece of feedback can belong to more than one category simultaneously — for instance, a coach saying “that was an excellent drive, but your follow-through was cut short” is extrinsic, partly positive, partly negative, and contains knowledge of performance.

Positive and Negative Feedback

Positive feedback confirms that an action was performed correctly. It reinforces the movement pattern in the performer’s memory, making it more likely to be repeated. A coach saying “great shoulder rotation on that serve” or a crowd applauding a clean strike are both positive feedback. For beginners especially, positive feedback is powerful — it builds confidence and keeps motivation high at a stage when errors are frequent and self-belief is fragile.

Negative feedback highlights what went wrong and, ideally, what should be done differently. The term “negative” does not mean unkind or demoralising — it simply means the feedback signals a mismatch between what was intended and what was produced. A rugby coach who tells a player “your tackling angle is too narrow, step out wider next time” is giving negative feedback that is precise and constructive. Elite performers often seek and welcome negative feedback because they are confident enough to use it as a tool rather than a threat.

Key Fact

Positive feedback is especially important for beginners because it builds confidence and reinforces correct movements. Negative feedback becomes more valuable for elite performers, who need precise detail on how to refine already high-level technique.

Intrinsic and Extrinsic Feedback

Intrinsic feedback (also called internal feedback) comes from the performer’s own body. It travels through sensory channels: proprioception (the sense of where your limbs are in space), vision, touch and hearing. A gymnast knows her balance beam routine felt fluent because her proprioceptive system reports smooth weight transfer and correctly timed muscle contractions. A cricketer senses from the impact vibration through the bat handle whether the ball was struck from the middle of the bat. Intrinsic feedback is instantaneous and continuous — it arrives during and immediately after every movement.

For intrinsic feedback to be useful, the performer must have the experience and body awareness to interpret the sensations correctly. Beginners often struggle to do this — they may feel that a movement went well when it did not, because they lack the kinaesthetic reference point of what “correct” feels like. Elite athletes, by contrast, are highly attuned to intrinsic feedback: Mo Farah described being able to sense the precise moment his running economy started to drop in the final 200 m of a 5,000 m race.

Extrinsic feedback (external feedback) originates outside the performer. Sources include coaches and teachers, peers, video analysis, heart rate monitors, scoreboards and the crowd. Because it comes from outside, extrinsic feedback can fill the gaps that intrinsic feedback misses — for example, a sprinter cannot feel the exact angle of her block start, but her coach can see it on a camera and give precise corrections.

A common error is assuming that because intrinsic feedback is immediate, it must be accurate. Beginners lack the kinaesthetic memory to judge “correct” feeling — a novice swimmer may feel that her arm entry is clean when it is actually crossed over the midline. This is precisely why extrinsic feedback from a coach or video is so critical in early learning: it provides a reliable external reference point until the performer builds a more accurate internal model.

Knowledge of Results and Knowledge of Performance

Knowledge of results (KR) tells the performer what the outcome was: the shot went wide, the javelin landed at 42 metres, the race was completed in 13.8 seconds. It is always extrinsic because the result is separate from the movement itself. KR is easy to understand and motivating — seeing a time improve from 14.2 s to 13.8 s gives a clear signal that training is working — but it tells the performer nothing about why the result was what it was, or how to change it.

Knowledge of performance (KP) focuses on the quality of the movement: the hips rotated too early, the release angle was too flat, the elbow position was correct. KP is richer than KR and more directly actionable because it tells the performer what to change. A coach watching a discus thrower and saying “your pivot foot twisted before your non-throwing arm swept across — you lost rotation” is giving knowledge of performance. Elite performers typically benefit more from KP because their outcomes are already competitive and fine technical detail is what separates them from rivals.

Key Fact

Knowledge of results (KR) = the outcome (time, score, distance). Knowledge of performance (KP) = the quality of the technique. KR motivates; KP teaches. Elite performers need both, but KP is the more powerful learning tool.

Choosing the Right Feedback for the Performer

The effectiveness of feedback depends on the performer’s stage of learning. Beginners benefit most from positive feedback (to build confidence), extrinsic feedback (because intrinsic awareness is unreliable), and knowledge of results (which is simple to understand). Overloading a beginner with detailed KP can cause confusion and undermine motivation.

Elite performers, on the other hand, respond best to specific negative and positive feedback on technique (KP), as well as their own well-developed intrinsic feedback. They also benefit from extrinsic sources such as video analysis and data from performance monitoring equipment. The key principle is that feedback should always be actionable — vague comments such as “try harder” or “that was good” without further detail have little learning value regardless of the performer’s level.

In the basic information processing model you studied in the previous lesson, feedback is the final stage that loops back into the input. Intrinsic feedback feeds into the system through the sensory display (sight, touch, proprioception). Extrinsic feedback arrives as a new input — the coach’s voice or the video replay enters the input stage alongside environmental information from the display. Both types then influence decision making in the next attempt, helping the performer select a more appropriate motor response from long-term memory. This loop is why consistent, timely feedback speeds up skill acquisition.
exam_tip_html: On a 2 marks — Define question, you need a precise one-sentence definition. “Positive feedback is good feedback” earns nothing — you must specify what it does (reinforces correct actions) and when it is most effective (for beginners). For a 4 marks — Explain question, give the definition (1 mark), explain the mechanism (1 mark), add the sporting example (1 mark), then link to the level of performer (1 mark). A very common error on feedback questions is confusing intrinsic/extrinsic (the source) with positive/negative (the tone) — these are separate dimensions and should never be swapped. On a 6 marks — Analyse question about feedback types, avoid bullet-pointing: instead write a developed paragraph that states a feedback type, explains what it does, applies it to a sporting context and evaluates its strengths and limitations.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Feedback has three dimensions: emotional tone (positive or negative), source (intrinsic or extrinsic), and what it tells you (knowledge of results or knowledge of performance). These categories overlap — a single piece of feedback can fit all three simultaneously.
  • Beginners benefit most from positive, extrinsic feedback and simple knowledge of results; elite performers gain more from specific, technique-focused knowledge of performance and their own well-developed intrinsic feedback.
  • Feedback must be actionable to have learning value — vague praise or criticism does not help performers identify what to change or repeat.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes knowledge of performance?
A) The time taken to complete a race
B) The score achieved in a gymnastics routine
C) The technical quality of the movements used to produce an outcome
D) The crowd reaction to an athlete's performance
practice_questions.marks: C) The technical quality of the movements used to produce an outcome [1 mark]

1 mark for identifying that intrinsic feedback comes from within the performer / the performer's own body / senses; 1 mark for naming the sensory mechanism involved (proprioception / kinaesthetic sense / sight / touch) or stating it is received during or immediately after movement. Example: 'Intrinsic feedback is information received from within the performer's own body — through proprioception and other senses — about how a movement felt during or immediately after its execution.'

practice_questions.text: Describe how knowledge of results and knowledge of performance each help an athlete improve. Use a sporting example in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for explaining knowledge of results — information about the outcome (score, time, distance) that tells the performer whether they succeeded or not; 1 mark for explaining knowledge of performance — information about the quality of the movement or technique used, pointing to what needs to change; 1 mark for a relevant sporting example that illustrates either or both (e.g. a high jumper learning their bar clearance height is KR, while being told their Fosbury flop arch needs to be higher is KP).

practice_questions.text: Explain why positive feedback is particularly important for beginner performers in physical activity.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining positive feedback as information that tells the performer what they did correctly; 1 mark for explaining that it reinforces the correct movement pattern in memory, making repetition more likely; 1 mark for linking to the beginner context — beginners make frequent errors and their confidence and motivation can be fragile, so reinforcing what is right encourages continued participation; 1 mark for a specific sporting example or further development (e.g. a beginner swimmer is told 'your arm entry was straight' — this confirms a technique she should repeat and helps her build a reliable kinaesthetic reference point).

practice_questions.text: A volleyball coach is working with two different groups: a Year 7 class learning to serve for the first time, and a county under-18 team preparing for a regional final. Analyse how the coach should adapt the type and focus of feedback given to each group.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies and explains at least two contrasting feedback strategies for each group, linking each to a specific reason grounded in the difference between beginners and elite performers. Applies consistent sporting examples to the volleyball context. Recognises that feedback type (positive/negative, intrinsic/extrinsic, KR/KP) varies systematically with experience level. Writes in developed prose rather than bullet points.

Secure: Identifies appropriate feedback for each group with some explanation. At least one reference to a specific feedback type (e.g. KP more useful for elite). Sporting application present but may be brief.

Developing: Makes relevant points about beginners needing simpler or more encouraging feedback, but development is limited. May describe rather than analyse. Sporting application minimal or absent.

Emerging: Basic points only (e.g. 'give more positive feedback to beginners'). No sporting application and limited development.

practice_questions.text: A 15-year-old county-level javelin thrower is told by his coach: 'Your run-up speed was good, but your elbow dropped below shoulder height at release — that cost you distance.' Identify and explain two types of feedback present in this statement.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that positive feedback is present ('run-up speed was good'); 1 mark for explaining that this reinforces the correct run-up technique so the athlete repeats it; 1 mark for identifying that negative feedback is present ('elbow dropped below shoulder height') or that knowledge of performance is present (the feedback is about technique quality not outcome); 1 mark for explaining that this gives the performer a specific technical target to correct in the next throw. (Accept identification of extrinsic feedback and explanation that it comes from the coach, not from the athlete's own sensations.)

knowledge_checks.q: Which type of feedback comes from within the performer's own body?
A sprinter is told her finishing time was 12.4 seconds. What type of feedback is this?
_____ feedback identifies an error in performance and points out what needs to change.
Knowledge of performance focuses on the _____ of the movement, not just the outcome.
Match each feedback type to its description:
right: Information confirming a correct action so it is repeated
Information about the outcome — score, time or distance achieved
Information received from a coach, video or another outside source

flashcard_questions.q: What is feedback in a sporting context?
flashcard_questions.a: Information about the outcome or quality of a movement, used to improve future performance.

flashcard_questions.q: What does positive feedback do to a movement pattern?
flashcard_questions.a: Reinforces it, making the performer more likely to repeat the correct action.

flashcard_questions.q: What does negative feedback tell a performer?
flashcard_questions.a: What went wrong and what needs to change — not that they performed badly.

flashcard_questions.q: For beginners, which emotional tone of feedback is most important and why?
flashcard_questions.a: Positive feedback — it builds confidence when errors are frequent.
Feedback from within the performer's own body, via proprioception and other senses.

flashcard_questions.q: Why can beginners not rely on intrinsic feedback alone?
flashcard_questions.a: They lack kinaesthetic experience to judge what 'correct' feels like.

flashcard_questions.q: Give two sources of extrinsic feedback in sport.
flashcard_questions.a: A coach's verbal instruction and video analysis replay.
Feedback about the outcome — the score, time or distance achieved.
Feedback about the quality of the technique or movement used.

flashcard_questions.q: Which type of performer benefits more from knowledge of performance: beginner or elite?
flashcard_questions.a: Elite performers — they need precise technical detail to improve already high-level skills.

flashcard_questions.q: Is knowledge of results always extrinsic?
flashcard_questions.a: Yes — the outcome (score, time, distance) comes from outside the performer's body.

flashcard_questions.q: A coach says 'your elbow position was perfect at release.' Which feedback types does this combine?
flashcard_questions.a: Positive feedback and knowledge of performance.

glossary_terms.definition: Information received about the outcome or quality of a movement or performance, used to improve future actions.
Feedback that tells a performer what they did correctly, reinforcing the action so it is repeated.
Feedback that identifies an error or weakness in performance, pointing out what needs to change.
Feedback that comes from within the performer, through the senses — touch, proprioception, sight and sound.
Feedback that comes from an outside source — a coach, a teammate, a video replay, or the scoreboard.
Feedback about the outcome of a movement — the score, distance, time or result achieved.
Feedback about the quality of the movement itself — the technique, timing or mechanics that produced the result.

items.title: High Performance Podcast — Sarina Wiegman on Developing Players Through Feedback
items.description: England's head coach discusses how she gives specific knowledge of performance to individual players and adjusts feedback style to each athlete's personality.

items.title: Don't Tell Me the Score — The Psychology of Coaching Feedback
items.description: Simon Mundie explores how positive and negative feedback are used differently at elite level, and why knowledge of performance beats knowledge of results for skill development.

items.title: How to Practice Effectively — TED-Ed
items.description: Illustrates how feedback loops during practice — both intrinsic feel and extrinsic coaching cues — are essential to skill acquisition at any level.

items.title: The Happy Secret to Better Work — Shawn Achor | TED
items.description: Achor's research on positive reinforcement and feedback shows why positive feedback builds confidence and motivation, especially in developing performers.

items.title: The Power of Believing You Can Improve — Carol Dweck | TED
items.description: Dweck shows how the type of feedback given to learners — focused on effort and technique (KP) rather than outcomes (KR) — shapes long-term development and resilience.

items.title: The Last Dance (2020)
items.description: Michael Jordan's demanding relationship with coaches and his response to extremely direct negative feedback illustrates how elite performers use critical knowledge of performance as a learning tool.

items.title: Coach Carter (2005)
items.description: Carter's coaching style — structured feedback, clear expectations and both positive and constructive criticism — shows the impact of well-applied feedback on young athletes.

items.title: BBC Bitesize — Types of Feedback in PE
items.description: AQA-aligned revision notes on positive/negative feedback, intrinsic/extrinsic feedback and knowledge of results vs knowledge of performance, with examples.

items.title: tutor2u — Feedback in Sport Revision Notes
items.description: Concise GCSE PE notes distinguishing feedback types and linking their use to beginner and elite performer contexts, with exam question practice.
